findings.summary: PPTX export aborts entirely when a single image fetch fails, unlike the PDF path which degrades gracefully
findings.evidence: `fetchImage: async (src) => { const blob = await docsImageFetcher(src); ... }` has no try/catch, and `docsImageFetcher` throws on any non-ok response (export-utils.ts:52-54). `exportPptx` awaits it inside the pre-scan loop (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:162) with no catch, so one deleted/403/CORS-failing image makes the whole export reject and the user gets "Export failed". The sibling PDF exporter deliberately tolerates this: resolveDeckImages catches per-image and substitutes BLANK_PNG (packages/slides/src/export/pdf.ts:277-283). Same user action, same deck, inconsistent all-or-nothing failure.

mergedFrom.summary: No progress feedback during the image-fetch phase of PPTX export; the toast only appears once slide serialization starts
mergedFrom.evidence: `exportPptx` fetches every unique image sequentially (index.ts:161-166) BEFORE the first `onProgress?.(0, slideTotal, 'slides')` at index.ts:272. For an image-heavy deck the user sees only a spinning trigger with no toast for the entire (potentially long, network-bound) fetch phase, and `yieldToPaint` is not called in that loop either, so the awaits are the only chance to paint. The PDF path has the same structure, so this is a pre-existing pattern, but the new code inherits it.

findings.summary: `blob.type || "image/png"` can mislabel non-PNG bytes as PNG, producing a media part whose extension/content-type contradicts its bytes
findings.evidence: `mime: blob.type || "image/png"` is fed into `extFromMime` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:163, 82-98), which also defaults unknown MIMEs to 'png'. If the backend serves an image with an empty or generic type (e.g. application/octet-stream) or an unsupported one (image/svg+xml, image/avif), the JPEG/SVG bytes are written to ppt/media/imageN.png and declared image/png via the [Content_Types].xml Default, which PowerPoint may reject or fail to render. A sniff of the leading bytes, or propagating the src extension, would be safer than defaulting to png.

findings.summary: `if (exporting) return` reads a stale closure value; the re-entrancy guard relies on `disabled` rather than the check itself
findings.evidence: `runExport` closes over the `exporting` state from the render in which the menu item was created. Two selects dispatched in the same tick would both see `exporting === false` and both start an export (double download, interleaved toast ids). In practice the dropdown closes on select and the items are `disabled={exporting}`, so this is unlikely to fire; a ref-based guard would be exact.

findings.summary: New PPTX export path feeds unvalidated, document-controlled image `src` into a credentialed fetch, then embeds the response bytes into the downloaded artifact
findings.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes each `ImageElement.data.src` straight to `docsImageFetcher` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:46-56), which does `fetch(resolveImageUrl(src), { credentials: "include" })` with no scheme/host allowlist (resolveImageUrl at export-utils.ts:12-18 explicitly preserves ANY absolute scheme). Image `src` is free-form text in the CRDT deck (packages/slides/src/model/element.ts:301-303) and is writable by any collaborator on a shared deck, or via the REST `PUT` content endpoint now documented for slides (packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md "Document Content (docs and slides)"). Attack chain: (a) attacker sets `src` to `http://attacker/px` — the victim's export issues a request from the victim's browser/network (internal/localhost hosts reachable, e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/...`), confirming the export ran and hitting non-CORS-protected GET endpoints on the victim's LAN; (b) attacker sets `src` to a same-origin authenticated endpoint (e.g. `/api/v1/workspaces/<wid>/documents/<did>/content`) — `docsImageFetcher` fetches it with the victim's cookies and `exportPptx` writes the raw bytes into `ppt/media/imageN.png` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-166, extFromMime falls back to `png` for any MIME), so private response bodies are exfiltrated into the file the victim then shares back. The header comment's claim that "backend images are same-origin-fetched with cookies" is also wrong: resolveImageUrl prefixes VITE_BACKEND_API_URL, so cookies are sent cross-origin. Pre-existing in the PDF path, but this diff adds a second, wider sink with no validation.

findings.summary: New datasources doc gives a false security assurance: it claims collaborators must "run their own connection", but any workspace member can execute queries with the creator's stored credentials
findings.evidence: The added page states "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." The code contradicts this: `POST datasources/:id/query` only calls `workspaceService.assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId)` (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:139-144) and then `executeQuery` connects with the stored, decrypted password (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:203). The frontend exposes it to any member via `executeDataSourceQuery` (packages/frontend/src/api/datasources.ts:100-107). So every workspace member is a confused deputy able to run arbitrary SELECTs against the creator's database with the creator's DB credentials. Users who read this doc will store personal/production DB credentials believing teammates cannot use them.

findings.summary: Doc added in this change presents the SSL toggle as a security control while the backend disables TLS certificate verification for datasource connections
findings.evidence: packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md instructs "SSL — toggle on if your database requires it", implying an encrypted, authenticated channel. `createClient` sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`, so the server accepts any certificate — an on-path attacker can MITM the connection and capture the datasource username/password and all query results. The new documentation advertises the feature without noting that verification is off.

findings.summary: safeFilename (extended for pptx in this diff) does not strip control characters or Unicode bidi overrides, allowing download-filename extension spoofing
findings.evidence: The sanitizer only removes `[\\/:*?"<>|]`. A document title containing U+202E (RTL override), NUL/newline, or a leading dot survives: a title like `report‮xcod.pptx` yields a download whose displayed name ends in `.docx`/is otherwise misleading, and control characters pass through to the `a.download` attribute (line 65). Since attackers can control document titles on shared documents, the victim can be tricked about what kind of file they just downloaded. Hardening: strip `[�-‎‏‪-‮⁦-⁩]` and leading dots as well.

findings.summary: Datasource connect flow has no host/port allowlist — server-side SSRF/internal port scanning — and the newly added doc contains no warning for self-hosters
findings.evidence: `createClient` connects to any user-supplied `host`/`port` from the backend (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:190-208), and `testConnection` returns the raw driver error message to the caller (line 121), which is a reliable oracle for distinguishing open/closed/filtered internal ports and reachable internal Postgres instances (e.g. `169.254.169.254`, `10.0.0.0/8`, container-internal hosts). Any authenticated workspace member can drive it. I found no allowlist, denylist, or private-IP check anywhere in the datasource module, and the new documentation page this change adds instructs users to enter arbitrary Host/Port with no self-hosting security note.

findings.summary: Neither the new datasources page nor the updated collaboration page warns that cached datasource query results are shown to anonymous share-link viewers
findings.evidence: `shared-document.tsx:188-189` renders `<DataSourceView readOnly>` for public `/shared/{token}` viewers; in readOnly mode execution is blocked (packages/frontend/src/app/spreadsheet/datasource-view.tsx:85) but the last persisted result rows are still displayed. The new datasources doc says only that "Collaborators can see the query and its last results", and the collaboration page updated in this change describes link sharing with "no account required for recipients" — so a user following these docs can publish live database output to an unauthenticated link without realising it.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

samples.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes each `ImageElement.data.src` straight to `docsImageFetcher` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:46-56), which does `fetch(resolveImageUrl(src), { credentials: "include" })` with no scheme/host allowlist (resolveImageUrl at export-utils.ts:12-18 explicitly preserves ANY absolute scheme). Image `src` is free-form text in the CRDT deck (packages/slides/src/model/element.ts:301-303) and is writable by any collaborator on a shared deck, or via the REST `PUT` content endpoint now documented for slides (packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md "Document Content (docs and slides)"). Attack chain: (a) attacker sets `src` to `http://attacker/px` — the victim's export issues a request from the victim's browser/network (internal/localhost hosts reachable, e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/...`), confirming the export ran and hitting non-CORS-protected GET endpoints on the victim's LAN; (b) attacker sets `src` to a same-origin authenticated endpoint (e.g. `/api/v1/workspaces/<wid>/documents/<did>/content`) — `docsImageFetcher` fetches it with the victim's cookies and `exportPptx` writes the raw bytes into `ppt/media/imageN.png` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-166, extFromMime falls back to `png` for any MIME), so private response bodies are exfiltrated into the file the victim then shares back.
